Method sheet / Index calculus and covers

Decomposing a hyperelliptic Jacobian

Two computations often share the word decomposition. One writes divisor classes as sums of small factor-base classes for index calculus. The other splits the Jacobian, up to isogeny, into lower-dimensional factors. A cover map can connect an elliptic DLP to either route, but it has its own field and subgroup checks. All 922 atlas curves now have a filterable, thirteen-property detection record.

01 / Cover and subgroup

Fix the group being attacked

The atlas binds 917 exact source-checker certificates to full curve identities. Each exposes the hyperelliptic equation coefficients, map polynomials, genus, degree and declared field. Five prime-field equations use a separately labeled algebraic replay of the same explicit formula. Browse these through the Hyperelliptic property filter or download the property index ↗.

For an elliptic source group, construct an exact map φ: H → E and record the field over which it is defined. Pullback and norm induce maps between E and Jac(H) with φ_* φ^* = [deg φ]. If the map degree is coprime to the chosen prime subgroup order, pullback is injective there. Otherwise check its kernel on that subgroup directly.

A discrete logarithm posed directly in Jac(H) starts at the next step. The existing same-field genus-two cover certificates already imply an elliptic quotient related to the source curve; that quotient alone does not identify a cheaper solver. A lower-field model that covers an elliptic curve only after field extension may have no corresponding elliptic factor over the lower field.

Published route / Joux–Vitse

Descend through an intermediate field

Joux and Vitse combine a cover H/F(p^n) → E/F(p^(nd)), defined after extension, with a norm–pullback map into Jac(H)(F(p^n)). The selected subgroup must meet that map’s kernel trivially. Their factor base uses points of H whose abscissae lie in F(p); verified divisor relations, sparse linear algebra and target descent complete the route. The atlas screens F(p^6)/F(p²)/F(p) with genus three and F(p^6)/F(p³)/F(p) with genus two separately.

For an odd-characteristic genus-three destination over F(p²), their bihomogeneous sieve saturates away trivial inverse-pair relations before counting eight-point full relations. The genus-two F(p³) branch needs its own decomposition solver; the quadratic sieve screen does not certify it. A positive cubic model label in this atlas is an input to cover construction, with the lower-field map, selected-subgroup transport and natural relation yield still to verify.

The paper’s worked F(p^6) case uses p=33,554,467, a 149-bit prime subgroup, a genus-three cover over F(p²), and a factor base of 16,775,441 points. It reports relation collection over 62 hours on 1,024 cores and iterative linear algebra over about 28.5 days on 64 cores. This is a source-reported campaign, indexed separately from the 922 local atlas identities. Download its exact field and curve parameters ↗

02 / Divisor relations

Build and solve an index calculus system

Represent reduced divisor classes in the declared curve and field model, using Mumford data where applicable. Freeze a factor base of small-degree prime divisors. Count how often independently sampled classes decompose over that base, verify each relation, and measure new linear rank. A large-prime variant keeps partial relations and recombines them through a collision graph.

Carry the computation through final sparse linear algebra and a previously unseen target’s descent. Report query law, all attempts including failures, full and partial relation yield, rank, memory, phase costs, and scalar replay. The published small-genus decomposition and double-large-prime methods are distinct choices; high-genus smoothness changes the cost regime.

Research: Sarkar–Singh divisor decomposition ↗Gaudry–Thomé–Thériault–Diem large primes ↗Enge high-genus algorithm ↗

03 / Jacobian factors

Screen a split, then construct the projection

Compute the exact Weil polynomial over the intended destination field. A factorization is a structural screen. To use a lower-dimensional factor, construct the isogeny and projections, record their degrees and kernels, and check the chosen generator and target images. If the factor appears only after scalar extension, price the route over that extension.

For a genus-two curve with a suitable elliptic subcover, its Jacobian splits up to isogeny as two elliptic factors. For a genus-three elliptic quotient, the complementary factor has dimension two and needs its own split or solver test. Report the actual subgroup image and total transfer-plus-solve cost before assigning an attack finding.
